title: docker-compose JWT_SECRET default does not match the value checked by the security warning — admin tokens are forgeable with a repo-published key and no warning is ever printed
evidence: docker-compose.yml:15 `      - JWT_SECRET=${JWT_SECRET:-CHANGE-ME-JWT-SECRET}`  vs. backend/internal/config/config.go:63 `JWTSecret:          getenv("JWT_SECRET", "change-me-jwt-secret"),` and backend/cmd/server/main.go:188 `if cfg.JWTSecret == "change-me-jwt-secret" {`. The compose default string is UPPERCASE; the startup check compares against the lowercase Go default, so the equality test can never match the value compose injects.
impact: Any deployment started with the stock compose file and no JWT_SECRET in the environment/.env signs admin JWTs with the literal string `CHANGE-ME-JWT-SECRET`, published in this public repository. An unauthenticated attacker crafts `{"uid":1,"uname":"admin","exp":<future>}` HS256-signed with that key and sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; backend/internal/admin/middleware.go:23 `claims, err := auth.Parse(s.secret, token)` accepts it (alg is pinned to HMAC, so no alg confusion is needed — the key itself is the vulnerability) and grants the full admin API: provider API keys (decrypted), config export, backup download, gateway keys, audit data. Because main.go:188 never matches and configstatus.go contains no default-value check, the deployment is silent — operators get neither a log warning nor any UI indication, so the 'defaults are warn-only' assumption that bounds this risk in the rest of the audit does NOT hold for the documented container path. (.env.template:21 uses the lowercase value, so the warning only fires for users who copy the template — the fallback path is the unprotected one.)
mitigations_checked: auth/jwt.go:31 pins SigningMethodHMAC (`if _, ok := t.Method.(*jwt.SigningMethodHMAC); !ok {`) so 'none'/RS256-submission confusion is not possible; warnInsecureDefaults (main.go:187-194) exists but its literal does not match the compose default; no other default-value detection anywhere (grep of `CHANGE-ME-JWT-SECRET` finds only docker-compose.yml:15); no JWT issuer/audience pinning that could constrain cross-service tokens; tokens carry no jti so nothing can be denied after the fact.
recommendation: Make the fail-safe symmetric: (1) set docker-compose.yml to `JWT_SECRET=${JWT_SECRET:?JWT_SECRET must be set}` (compose already uses this pattern for REDIS_PASSWORD at line 37) so a default can never be used; (2) replace the string-literal comparison in warnInsecureDefaults with a set of known-insecure values (both cases of the placeholder plus the Go default) or, better, refuse to boot in Release mode when JWT_SECRET is a known placeholder; (3) additionally log the SHA-256 prefix of the active secret at startup so operators can confirm what is really in use.

title: No session revocation anywhere: 24h stateless JWT survives logout, password change, MFA disable and admin-side unbind; middleware never re-validates the user
evidence: auth.go:152-155 `func (s *Server) logout(c *gin.Context) { s.recordOp(c, "login", "auth", "logout", nil, nil); s.ok(c, nil) }` — logout only writes an audit row. auth.go:181 `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Update("password_hash", string(hash))` — password change does not invalidate previously issued tokens. auth.go:278-279 and users.go:48-49 clear the MFA secret without touching sessions. backend/internal/auth/jwt.go:21 `ExpiresAt: jwt.NewNumericDate(time.Now().Add(24 * time.Hour)),` — no `ID`/jti claim at all (Claims struct, jwt.go:11-15, has only UserID/Username/RegisteredClaims), and grep for `jti|revok|blacklist|token_version` across backend/ returns nothing. backend/internal/admin/middleware.go:23-30 only parses the JWT and sets context — no DB lookup of the user row.
impact: A stolen token (from `localStorage['llm-router-guard.auth.v1']` via any XSS, from a reverse-proxy access log for the WS endpoint at backend/internal/admin/auditws.go:31 `claims, err := auth.Parse(s.secret, c.Query("token"))` which accepts the admin JWT in a URL query string, or from a lost laptop) is a 24-hour full-admin credential that cannot be withdrawn. The incident-response sequence that should stop an intrusion — logout, change the password, unbind MFA, unlock the account — changes nothing for the attacker, and every one of those actions looks 'successful' in the UI. Because the middleware never loads the user row, even deleting/locking the account leaves the bearer authorized. The absence of a token version/jti also means there is no mechanism to add revocation later without a schema change.
mitigations_checked: alg confusion is blocked (jwt.go:31 HMAC type assertion); expiry is enforced by golang-jwt v5 default validators; JWT is not stored in a cookie and there is no CORS middleware, so a cross-origin page cannot silently attach it — which is why the WS endpoint's query-string token is not cross-site-hijackable but is log/cache-exposable; frontend does call POST /auth/logout (MainLayout.tsx:184-192), so the client 'believes' the session ends.
recommendation: Add a `token_version uint` column to admin_users, put it in Claims, bump it in issueLogin-adjacent sensitive operations (logout, changePassword, mfaDisable, unbindUserMfa, unlockUser, account delete) and compare it in AuthMiddleware after loading the user; or keep a short-lived access token (5-15 min) with a refresh token stored server-side in the existing mfaStore/Redis. For /audit/ws, accept the token in a subprotocol header or a short-lived one-time WS ticket instead of a long-lived JWT in the query string.

title: Unauthenticated attacker can permanently lock the sole admin out of the console (lockout DoS): account lockout keyed on username with no per-IP limit, and failed_logins is never reset when the lock expires
evidence: routes.go:42 `api.POST("/auth/login", s.login)` — no rate-limit middleware on the login route (the quota.RateLimiter/RedisLimiter is gateway-API-key scoped only; see quota/quota.go:55 `func (rl *RateLimiter) Allow(snap *runtime.Snapshot, apiKeyID uint, alias string)`). auth.go:76-79 `if err := bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword(...); err != nil { s.onMFAFail(&u); ... }` and auth.go:114-121 `func (s *Server) onMFAFail(u *model.AdminUser) { u.FailedLogins++; updates := map[string]any{"failed_logins": u.FailedLogins}; if u.FailedLogins >= 5 { loc := time.Now().Add(15 * time.Minute); updates["locked_until"] = loc } ... }`. model.go:28-30 `func (u *AdminUser) IsLocked() bool { return u.LockedUntil != nil && time.Now().Before(*u.LockedUntil) }` — the counter is only cleared by a successful login (auth.go:81-83) or by POST /users/:id/unlock (users.go:61-62).
impact: Lockout is keyed to the username, not the source address, so anyone on the network can spend the admin's 5 attempts with random passwords. Worse, because `failed_logins` is left at 5 after the 15-minute lock lapses, a single further wrong password immediately re-locks for another 15 minutes: a cron job sending one bogus password every ~15 minutes denies the legitimate admin access indefinitely. In a running incident the attacker uses this to keep the defender out of the console (cannot rotate provider keys, cannot disable a leaked gateway key, cannot read audit) while their own session — see authn-2 — is unaffected. There is no per-IP throttle, no CAPTCHA and no alert on lock events to make this visible.
mitigations_checked: lockout does exist (mitigates TOTP guessing: after 5 second-factor failures the account is locked, and the ticket branch at auth.go:46-70 also calls onMFAFail); a legitimate operator can clear it directly on the DB, and /users/:id/unlock exists; SQLite `SetMaxOpenConns(1)` (db/db.go:52) serializes writes but does not prevent cross-request state loss.
recommendation: Add a per-IP (and per-username+IP) token-bucket limiter in front of /auth/login, reset `failed_logins` when `locked_until` passes (treat the lock as the end of the counter's life), require a non-guessable login identifier (or return lock state only after correct credentials), and alert/audit-notify on lock events so an operator sees the DoS rather than assuming they mistyped their password.

title: failed_logins is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent login requests defeat the 5-attempt lockout and allow large-scale online password guessing
evidence: auth.go:34 `if err := s.db.Where("username = ?", req.Username).First(&u).Error; err != nil {` loads the row; auth.go:115-121 then writes a Go-side increment: `u.FailedLogins++` … `updates := map[string]any{"failed_logins": u.FailedLogins}` … `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Updates(updates)`. There is no `gorm.Expr("failed_logins + 1")`, no transaction and no row lock (the same pattern also drops concurrent recovery-code consumption — see authn-9).
impact: With K parallel wrong-password requests all reading `failed_logins = N`, every one of them writes `N+1`; the winner is arbitrary and the effective counter advances by 1 per burst instead of K. An attacker therefore gets an essentially unbounded number of password guesses (a burst of 50-200 concurrent POSTs per 'attempt' of the counter) with no per-IP limit (authn-3) — bcrypt cost 10 is a few tens of milliseconds of CPU per attempt, so dictionary/credential-stuffing attacks against `admin` succeed at practical rates. The lockout that the code (REQ-022) and docs present as the brute-force defence is not a real control.
mitigations_checked: the value written is always a valid integer (no negative/overflow path); successful login resets it (auth.go:81-83); `locked_until` is compared with server time (model.go:29), so no client-side bypass; GORM `TranslateError: true` and WAL are on but provide no isolation across the read/write pair.
recommendation: Do the increment in SQL — `UpdateColumn("failed_logins", gorm.Expr("failed_logins + 1"))` — and read the resulting value back (or lock the row in a transaction) before deciding to set `locked_until`; better, move the failure counter to the shared mfaStore (Redis INCR + EXPIRE) so it is both atomic and multi-instance-safe.

title: Pre-authentication lock response distinguishes existing from non-existing usernames (enumeration oracle)
evidence: auth.go:34-37 unknown user: `s.fail(c, http.StatusUnauthorized, 40102, "用户名或密码错误")`. auth.go:38-41 the lock check runs BEFORE any password verification and on the next line: `if u.IsLocked() { s.fail(c, http.StatusForbidden, 40301, "账户已被锁定，请稍后再试或联系管理员解锁")`. The two responses differ both in HTTP status (401 vs 403) and in business code (40102 vs 40301).
impact: An unauthenticated attacker submits 5 wrong passwords for a candidate username: a real account answers 403/40301, a non-existent one keeps answering 401/40102. That reliably enumerates valid admin usernames (and reveals lock state for defense evasion, letting the attacker time their guesses around the 15-minute window and know exactly when their lockout-DoS succeeded). It also lets them skip bcrypt work on names that do not exist, and it turns 'admin' vs custom ADMIN_USER names into a fingerprintable target list for the credential-stuffing described in authn-3/authn-4. The frontend deliberately hides this (Login.tsx:62-67 collapses 401/40102/40103 into one generic message), but the API exposes it to anyone with curl. A secondary, weaker variant of the same oracle exists in auth.go:52-55 ("MFA 票据与用户不匹配") which confirms a username→ID mapping to a holder of any ticket.
mitigations_checked: password failures and MFA failures both return generic messages; the response for a wrong password does not reveal whether MFA is configured (the `mfa_required` step is only reachable after bcrypt success, auth.go:86-92); login does not return timing-distinguishable branches beyond the bcrypt cost already paid for real users; no user-registration or password-reset endpoint exists that would leak names another way.
recommendation: Evaluate the lock state only after the password check succeeds (or always run a dummy bcrypt for unknown users and return one identical 401 envelope for 'unknown user', 'bad password' and 'locked'), and use the same code/message for all three; if a distinct lock message is required for UX, deliver it only to authenticated sessions.

title: "Require MFA for all users" is not enforced: login hands out a fully privileged token and only sets an advisory need_bind_mfa flag; nothing server-side gates unbound users
evidence: auth.go:133-138 `needBind := sec.MFAEnabled && sec.MFARequiredAll && !u.MFAEnabled` … `s.ok(c, gin.H{"token": token, "user": ..., "need_bind_mfa": needBind})` — the token is issued unconditionally, the flag is data only. middleware.go:14-31 validates nothing but the signature; it never looks at MFA state. settings/settings.go:87 `return Security{MFAEnabled: true, MFARequiredAll: false, RecoveryCodeCount: 10, GraceDays: 7}` — grep shows `GraceDays` has zero references anywhere in backend/ (declared, never used), and grep for MFARequiredAll finds only auth.go:133.
impact: With the console setting labelled '强制所有用户启用 MFA' / 'Require MFA for All Users' (i18n security.ts:8) an organisation believes every admin login is two-factor. In reality a user who never binds MFA — or an attacker who phishes/brute-forces the password of such an account (authn-3/authn-4 make this feasible) — authenticates with one factor and gets a token that passes every authorization check in the admin API, including the ones that change security policy. Skipping enrolment costs nothing: `curl -X POST /api/admin/v1/providers` with the returned token works; the only consequence is a client-side redirect to /account/security (Login.tsx:46-48) and a hint paragraph (AccountSecurity.tsx:314-318), both trivially bypassed by discarding the SPA and calling the REST API directly. There is also no server-side 'MFA enrollment required' blocking state, so even the 7-day grace period concept implied by GraceDays is unimplemented.
mitigations_checked: second factor IS enforced for users who have bound it (auth.go:86-108, and the ticket branch at auth.go:46-73 cannot be skipped by omitting totp_code — omitting it just returns a ticket, never a token); self-service bind/unbind requires a valid TOTP or recovery code (auth.go:236, auth.go:268-277); recovery codes are stored hashed (mfa.go:50); `mfaSetup` refuses to re-issue over an existing binding (auth.go:206-209).
recommendation: Gate the authenticated route group: in AuthMiddleware (or a second middleware) load the user and reject with a dedicated code (e.g. 40302) when `sec.MFAEnabled && sec.MFARequiredAll && !u.MFAEnabled` and the request is not one of the MFA-enrolment/password endpoints; or refuse to issue a privileged token until enrolment completes (issue a scoped 'enrolment-only' token). Implement or delete `grace_days` so the config surface matches behaviour, and stop naming the control 'require/强制' while it is advisory.

title: TOTP codes are accepted for 90 seconds with no replay suppression and no per-user 'last used step' — one observed code unlocks login, binding and unbinding repeatedly
impact: A code intercepted once — shoulder-surfing, a screenshot/AOD notification read by malware or a screen-share, a malicious authenticator backup, a proxy that observed a step-2 POST body — can be replayed by anyone for up to 90 seconds, any number of times, and for any purpose: complete a login (auth.go:94), bind a fresh attacker-chosen secret is not needed but *unbind* the victim's MFA (auth.go:268) to strip the second factor, and re-run login repeatedly inside the window to mint multiple admin JWTs (which, per authn-2, remain valid for 24 hours after the window closes). Because the same code also validates at the 'enable' step, an attacker who can get a user to enter a code while their account is mid-enrolment can confirm binding on a secret they already know. The 5-failure lockout limits guessing but not replay.
mitigations_checked: skew is the library default of 1 (not a widened custom window); 6 digits/SHA-1 matches Google Authenticator compatibility expectations; failed second-factor attempts increment the same lockout counter via onMFAFail (auth.go:67, auth.go:104); login tickets are single-use and 128-bit random (auth.go:88 `token := crypto.RandomHex(16)` with crypto/rand — crypto/crypto.go:74-78); TOTP is never compared to a user-supplied secret via `==`.
recommendation: Track the last accepted time-step per user (and per purpose: login / enable / disable) in the existing mfaStore — reject any step <= the stored one — and narrow the window with `totp.ValidateCustom(code, secret, time.Now().UTC(), otp.ValidateOpts{Period:30, Skew:0 or 1, Digits:6, Algorithm:SHA1})` after enforcing clock-drift monitoring; require the current code plus a re-authenticated password for destructive changes such as mfaDisable.

title: Default (in-memory) MFA ticket store implements no expiry at all — 2FA pre-auth tickets and pending TOTP setup secrets live forever, contradicting the documented uniform 5-minute TTL
evidence: redis_mfa.go:21-22 `// mfaStore MFA 短时效票据存储。Pop* 取出即作废（一次性）。\n// TTL 统一 5 分钟，替代原内存实现的 expiry 检查。` — but the memory implementation has no expiry and no sweeper: redis_mfa.go:37-44 `func (m *memMFA) SaveLoginTicket(token string, uid uint) { m.login.Store(token, uid) }` / `v, ok := m.login.LoadAndDelete(token)` and redis_mfa.go:45-52 for setup secrets; the struct is only `sync.Map`s (redis_mfa.go:32-35) with no timestamp field, while the Redis path does honour TTL (redis_mfa.go:56 `const mfaTicketTTL = 5 * time.Minute`, used at :93 and :111). redis_mfa.go:124-131 selects `&memMFA{}` whenever REDIS_ADDR is unset — which is the shipped default (docker-compose.yml:21 `REDIS_ADDR=${REDIS_ADDR:-}` and DB_TYPE=sqlite).
impact: On the default single-node deployment the second-factor session between 'password accepted' and 'TOTP accepted' never times out: a login ticket that is returned to the browser (auth.go:90 `s.ok(c, gin.H{"mfa_required": true, "mfa_token": token})`) and abandoned — or captured from a proxy log, a crash-dumped request body, or a shared machine — remains redeemable for the lifetime of the process, so the 90-second-second-factor UX assumption is replaced by 'whenever the attacker gets around to it' (combined with a replayed or observed code — authn-7 — this is a complete login). For the same reason the pending TOTP secret from /account/mfa/setup (auth.go:220 `s.mfa().SaveSetupSecret(uid, secret)`) stays redeemable indefinitely on the server, so an attacker who obtains that secret plus any current valid code can complete binding long after the intended window, and rows accumulate in memory for the lifetime of the process. Behaviour also diverges silently between the two stores (5 min vs ∞), so security testing done against a Redis deployment does not describe production SQLite deployments.
mitigations_checked: tickets are single-use and atomically popped in both backends (`LoadAndDelete`, and the Lua GET+DEL at redis_mfa.go:59-65), so double-spend of one ticket is not possible; ticket values are 128-bit random (auth.go:88); Redis keys are namespaced with a version prefix (`gw:mfa:login:v1:`, :85); a Redis outage degrades to memory with a logged warning (redis_mfa.go:76-80) rather than failing open on validation.
recommendation: Store `{value, expiresAt}` in memMFA and reject expired entries in Pop* (plus a periodic cleanup, or reuse the existing 5-minute constant), so both backends honour the documented TTL; return the mfa_token to the client only over a header/body that is never cached and instruct the SPA to drop it on step change.

title: Recovery codes: single-use not enforced (non-atomic consume) and stored as fast unsalted SHA-256 with a non-constant-time compare
evidence: mfa.go:63-75 `target := crypto.Sha256Hex(code)` … `for i, h := range list { if h == target {` … `next := append(list[:i:i], list[i+1:]...); return true, marshalRecoveryHashed(next)}` — the caller then writes the new JSON separately: auth.go:60-63 `if used, next := consumeRecoveryCode(req.RecoveryCode, u.RecoveryCodesJSON); used { ok2 = true; s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Update("recovery_codes_json", next) }` (same at auth.go:97-101 and auth.go:270-273), from the row loaded at auth.go:34 — no transaction, no `WHERE recovery_codes_json = <old>` guard. mfa.go:50 `hashed[i] = crypto.Sha256Hex(p)` with crypto/crypto.go:68-71 `sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(s))` (unsalted, single-round).
impact: Because the write is a read-modify-write of the whole JSON array, two concurrent logins that present the same recovery code both see it in the list and both reach `issueLogin` (auth.go:71/110): the 'single-use' property that makes an offline recovery code less dangerous than a TOTP seed does not hold, and the last writer silently restores the code the first one consumed. The same pattern also resurrects codes that were consumed by a parallel request, and `mfaDisable` (auth.go:270-273) can be passed a code that the user believes was burnt. Independently, codes are protected by an unsalted fast hash: anyone who obtains a DB file or a backup archive (the backup endpoint ships the raw SQLite file) can verify guesses at GPU speed against the bcrypt-hashed passwords as well — the 64-bit codes (mfa.go:47 `p := crypto.RandomHex(8)` → 16 hex chars) resist online guessing but not offline mass verification, and unlike the password hash there is no work factor.
mitigations_checked: generation uses crypto/rand (crypto/crypto.go:74-78 `_, _ = io.ReadFull(rand.Reader, b)`), so codes are not predictable; the slice-expression `append(list[:i:i], ...)` avoids aliasing corruption of the source slice; `countRecoveryLeft` (mfa.go:79-85) exposes only a count; recovery-code attempts increment the shared lockout counter (auth.go:67) so online brute force is throttled; codes are shown once (auth.go:248) and never logged (recordOp passes nil before/after).
recommendation: Consume in a single atomic statement — `UPDATE admin_users SET recovery_codes_json = ? WHERE id = ? AND recovery_codes_json = ?` and require 1 affected row (or use a dedicated recovery_codes table with `DELETE ... WHERE code_hash = ? RETURNING id`) — and store codes with bcrypt/scrypt or HMAC-SHA256 under a server-side key; keep the lockout counter shared as-is.

title: Bootstrap admin password lifecycle is broken: ADMIN_PASSWORD is silently ignored after first boot, the compose default suppresses the weak-password warning, and the DB file sits outside the mounted volume so the password silently reverts to admin123 on container recreation
evidence: main.go:164-169 `func bootstrapAdmin(gdb *gorm.DB, cfg *config.Config) { var count int64; gdb.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Count(&count); if count > 0 { return } }` — when users exist, ADMIN_PASSWORD is dropped on the floor with no log line. main.go:170-174 `pass := cfg.AdminPassword; if pass == "" { pass = "admin123"; log.Println("[bootstrap] WARNING: using default admin password 'admin123'. Set ADMIN_PASSWORD to change.") }` — the warning is gated on the empty string, but docker-compose.yml:18 always injects a value: `- ADMIN_PASSWORD=${ADMIN_PASSWORD:-admin123}` (and .env.template:28 ships `ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin123` uncommented), so under the documented deployment `pass` is never empty and the WARNING never fires even though the literal admin123 is used. Persistence: config.go:62 `DBDSN: getenv("DB_DSN", "gateway.db")` is a relative path resolved against Dockerfile:25 `WORKDIR /app` (i.e. /app/gateway.db), while docker-compose.yml:26 mounts only `${DATA_DIR_PATH:-./data}:/app/data` — the SQLite file (users, password hashes, sessions-independent JWT config, audit) is in the container layer, and `restart: unless-stopped` (compose:27) recreates it on rebuild/`down`/host move.
impact: Three compounding effects, all silent. (1) An operator who first boots with the compose default, is told to change the password, later adds a strong ADMIN_PASSWORD to .env and restarts, keeps admin123 forever — no warning, no error, the env var is simply unused. (2) A docker-compose deployment using defaults logs NOTHING about admin123 (the only guard in the codebase is the empty-string check) while README:56 asserts the default password is announced on the console, so nobody learns the console is reachable with a public credential on 0.0.0.0:8080 (compose:10). (3) Because the DB is not in the volume, any container re-creation wipes the account and re-bootstraps it with the compose value — an admin who rotated away from admin123 is transparently rotated BACK to the published default on the next `docker compose up`, with the log line at main.go:183 only reading 'created admin user: admin'. Combined with authn-3/authn-4 (no login rate limiting) and authn-6 (MFA not enforced), a known credential is enough for total compromise of the gateway and all upstream provider keys.
mitigations_checked: the password is bcrypt-hashed at creation (main.go:175, cost 10 = bcrypt.DefaultCost) and compared with the constant-time library helper; username uniqueness is enforced by `gorm:"uniqueIndex"` (model.go:15); changePassword exists (PUT /auth/password, routes.go:45) so rotation is possible; no default password is ever returned by an API. None of these address the silent-ignore/silent-restore behaviour.
recommendation: Require ADMIN_PASSWORD (or generate a random one printed once) instead of a shipped literal — `ADMIN_PASSWORD=${ADMIN_PASSWORD:?...}` in compose; log an ERROR (and optionally refuse to serve /api/admin/v1) when a login using the default literal succeeds; make bootstrap reconcile ADMIN_USER/ADMIN_PASSWORD with the DB (or explicitly log 'ADMIN_PASSWORD ignored: N users already exist'); move DB_DSN into the mounted volume (e.g. default `DB_DSN=/app/data/gateway.db`) so state and password changes survive re-creation; force a password change on first login for accounts still using the default.

title: Audit-log source IP is taken from an unvalidated X-Forwarded-For header, letting any client forge the IP recorded for logins, MFA changes and admin mutations
impact: This directly defeats the hardening described at main.go:90-94 — `// 仅信任配置内的反向代理；默认空 → 不解析 X-Forwarded-For，c.ClientIP() 取 TCP 对端` with `engine.SetTrustedProxies(cfg.TrustedProxies)` — because this helper bypasses gin's trust model entirely: the header is honoured for the audit path even when TRUSTED_PROXIES is empty. An attacker who authenticates (by brute force per authn-3/4, or with the default password per authn-10, or with a forged token per authn-1) sets `X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.5` and the operation log attributes their login and their MFA unbind / API-key creation to a benign internal address. The forensic value of REQ-003 audit — the mechanism an operator would use to detect a takeover, since sessions cannot be revoked (authn-2) — is destroyed, and the attacker can additionally inject arbitrary strings (including blank/space-padded or IPv6-looking values) into the IP column and into the CSV export of operations.
mitigations_checked: gateway-side decisions still use gin's trusted IP — the API-key IP allowlist path (model.go:42-44 `IPAllowlistJSON` / `IPAllowlistEnabled`) relies on `c.ClientIP()`, so this helper does not weaken gateway authorization; the app's own access log at main.go:116-117 prints `c.ClientIP()`, i.e. the correctly-validated peer address, so the header cannot plant a fake IP in stdout logs; the stored value is never used in any security decision inside admin (grep for `clientIP(` shows exactly the two sites above), so impact is limited to log poisoning / attribution.
recommendation: Delete the hand-rolled helper and use `c.ClientIP()` everywhere (gin already applies TRUSTED_PROXIES), or only consult X-Forwarded-For when `len(cfg.TrustedProxies) > 0`; validate the parsed value with `net.ParseIP` and store NULL plus the raw header (in a separate, clearly-untrusted column) when it does not parse.

title: changePassword ignores the bcrypt error: a new password longer than 72 bytes silently blanks password_hash, permanently locking the admin out with a success response and no reset path
evidence: auth.go:180-183 `hash, _ := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword([]byte(req.NewPassword), bcrypt.DefaultCost)` … `s.db.Model(&model.AdminUser{}).Where("id = ?", u.ID).Update("password_hash", string(hash))` … `s.ok(c, nil)`. The error is discarded; in the pinned dependency (go.mod:14 `golang.org/x/crypto v0.31.0`) bcrypt returns `ErrPasswordTooLong` — x/crypto@v0.31.0/bcrypt/bcrypt.go:87 `var ErrPasswordTooLong = errors.New("bcrypt: password length exceeds 72 bytes")` and :97 `return nil, ErrPasswordTooLong` — so `hash` is nil and `string(hash)` is `""`. The only length rule is auth.go:166-168 `if len(req.NewPassword) < 8 { s.fail(...) }` (minimum, no maximum).
impact: Setting a >72-byte passphrase (a perfectly reasonable long-phrase password, and exactly what password managers produce with a 96-char generator) writes an empty password_hash and answers 200/"ok". Every later login then fails closed: auth.go:76 `bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword([]byte(u.PasswordHash), []byte(req.Password))` returns `ErrHashTooShort` (x/crypto bcrypt.go:170) for the empty hash, so the branch always errors → 40102 forever, and the MFA ticket branch cannot help it. Since there is no administrative password-reset endpoint (routes.go exposes only /auth/password, /users/:id/unlock and /users/:id/unbind-mfa) and no CLI/reset command, the only recovery is direct SQL/DB-file surgery on a column named password_hash — in a single-admin deployment this is loss of the console, discovered only when the operator is locked out. The same bug means a transient bcrypt failure would be recorded as a successful password change.
mitigations_checked: the old password is verified before the update (auth.go:176-179), so this is self-inflicted, not attacker-triggerable; MFA remains enforced for bound accounts; the failure is fail-closed (no blank-password login is possible); no session/token side effect. The defect is availability + silent-success, not authentication bypass. Also noted: `admin123` (main.go:172) satisfies the 8-char minimum, and the policy has no composition/breach-list check.
recommendation: Handle the error (`if err != nil { s.fail(c, 400, 40001, "密码设置失败") ; return }`), reject NewPassword longer than 72 bytes with an explicit message, verify the hash is non-empty before writing, check the write's `RowsAffected`/error, and require that the new password differ from the old; ship an out-of-band reset (server subcommand or a documented single-user SQL migration) so a corrupted hash is recoverable.
